Description: SDMs often assume that a species is in equilibrium (or quasi-equilibrium) with the environment in which it occurs. That is, suitable habitat is fully occupied or saturated (e.g., Gallien et al. 2012, Zurell et al. 2024).
Violation: This assumption can be violated in several ways. For instance, the species range can be restricted by biotic interactions (e.g., competition, predation, pathogens, disturbances; Richmond et al. 2010), leaving portions of their suitable habitat unoccupied. In addition, for invasive species, the extent to which the invader occupies their suitable environment varies depending on the stage of invasion (Gallien et al. 2012). Dispersal barriers may also prevent invader and range-shifting species from reaching suitable habitats (Foster et al. 2022, Marjakangas et al. 2023; see criteria “No dispersal limitation”). There is also increasing evidence that range-shifting species are lagging behind their climatically suitable habitat (Svenning et al. 2008), leading to suitable habitat with delayed colonization (“colonisation credit”) and delayed extinction (“extinction debt”; Foden et al 2007, Foster et al. 2022, Zurell et al. 2024). Additionally, the chances of violating this criteria increase with the extent of the study region (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024).
Solutions: Use historical range information for model training., Develop a dispersal model to best estimate the species potential distribution (Merow et al. 2016)., Include species' ecological traits in SDMs (Hanspach et al. 2010; Jiguet et al. 2010; Viana & Chase 2022)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption., Can we use disequilibrium indicators (e.g. filled vs. unfilled regional niches) to predict a species' future spread or adaptation potential?., "Use models that incorporate biological processes (e.g. thermal limits, energetics) rather than just statistical correlations, as these better capture real-world limitations beyond simple climate.", "Add functions relating occurrence likelihood to distance from known locations to account for dispersal limitations and mass effects, improving niche models.", Implement Nested SDMs (N-SDMs; Guisan et al. 2025).
Justification: If a model assumes that suitable habitat is fully occupied when in fact it is not, it is well understood that the model may underestimate suitable habitat in areas with missing species presences in the model training step (Welk 2004, Richmond et al. 2010, Václavík & Meentemeyer 2012). Evidence also exists for overestimated suitable habitat in areas not occupied by the species (e.g., due to competition and dispersal limitation; Lowen et al. 2019).

Description: SDMs typically assume that species maintain their ecological niche (the set of environmental conditions they require to thrive) across space and time. That is, "the notion that the niche envelope is a fixed and immutable characteristic of a species, unchanging over space and time" (Wiens et al. 2009).
Violation: This assumption can be violated in several ways. For example, invasive species may develop adaptations to local conditions (biotic or abiotic) and thus occupy areas outside their native environmental niche (Gallien et al. 2012, Gallien et al. 2010, Weins et al. 2009). Ongoing and future climate change may also lead to rapid evolutionary (particularly in the case of short-generation species; Wiens et al. 2009, Franks et al. 2007) or behavioural adaptations to environmental conditions (e.g., changes in timing of spring migration or breeding activity in birds; Root et al. 2003). The probability of violation also depends on the speed of change, the forecasting horizon (i.e., long-term forecasts are more susceptible as greater evolutionary and/or behaviour change may accumulate), and the spatial extent of the analysis (the larger the extent, the greater the likelihood of non-stationarity; Pease et al. 2022).
Solutions: Shorten timescale of analysis., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.
Justification: For prediction models, under and overestimation can occur, but are dependent on sampling and ecological context (Bryn et al. 2021). If local rapid adaptations are occurring within different populations of the study area – beyond disrupting the assumption of species-environment equilibrium – the species may respond differently to the predictor variables across the analysis extent. As a consequence, the model can both underestimate (e.g., by missing unique environmental tolerances that are locally relevant via over-smoothing) and overestimate (e.g., by assuming broader environmental tolerances than any local population is adapted to) suitable habitat (Guisan & Thuiller 2005). Similarly to forecasting-horizon, this is more likely to occur with a small sample size (Guisan & Thuiller 2005).

Description: The Eltonian noise hypothesis states that local biotic interactions do not alter species’ environmental niches at larger scales, only introduce statistical noise. Instead, species niche is assumed to be dominantly determined by climate (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). Most SDMs rely on this hypothesis and thus, often only include abiotic variables as predictors. Yet, biotic interactions are among the reasons why a species may not be at equilibrium with their environment (Richmond et al. 2010, Jeschke & Strayer 2008).
Violation: There is growing evidence that this assumption can be frequently violated, supported by improved SDMs when biotic interactions are included (e.g., Fern et al. 2019, Boulangeat et al. 2012, Godsoe & Harmon 2012, Suttle et al. 2007). In some cases (e.g., boreal caribou, wolf, and moose; Boutin et al. 2012), there is evidence that competition and/or predation restrict the distribution of species (Poggiato et al. 2025). In other cases, it is clear that mutualism and/or symbiosis allow species to persist. By ignoring biotic interactions, SDMs may capture the Grinnellian (fundamental bioclimatic) niche instead of the Eltonian (realized biotic) niche (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). However, Godsoe & Harmon (2012) highlight that violation of this assumption is not universal. Instead, it depends on the species, type of biotic interaction, and modelling method (Araújo & Luoto 2007). Additionally, the chances of violating this criteria increase with the extent of the study region (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024).
Solutions: Include biotic interactions as predictors (Heikkinen et al. 2007)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.
Justification: In the case of positive interactions, models may overestimate a species distribution by predicting as suitable those areas within the preferred abiotic conditions but where its mutualistic or symbiotic partner is absent from (Boulangeat et al. 2012).

Description: SDMs should be built using occurrence data that are free of substantial errors regarding taxonomic identification (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024, Araújo et al. 2019, Aubry et al. 2017, Maldonado et al. 2015).
Violation: Despite the increasing accessibility to occurrence data via online biodiversity portals (e.g., GBIF, eBird, iNaturalis) and their attention to data quality and uncertainty, taxonomic misidentifications remain common (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). Additionally, many records lack information regarding the uncertainty of identification, and may often fail to capture updates in taxonomic publications (Anderson et al. 2020). Violations can also occur through direct data collection via misidentification in the field or mistakes during data entering.
Solutions: Implement partial vetting (Soley et al. 2024)., Standardize and clean data for given taxonomic groups and regions (Soley et al. 2024)., Remove occurrences without spatial reference., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.
Justification: When SDMs are built using occurrence data containing misidentified records, the foundational assumption that the data accurately represents a single biological entity is broken. In this case, the species-environmental relationships captured by the model represent an aggregated environmental envelope that belongs to no single species in nature, and can result in overestimation of suitable habitat for both prediction and projection models (e.g., Costa et al. 2015, Romero et al. 2014). The impact of misidentifications is expected to be more severe for rare and/or cryptic species (e.g., Aubry et al. 2017). For the related case of missing records, see criteria “Unbiased species data”.
Citations: Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Araújo et al. 2019; Aubry et al. 2017; Maldonado et al. 2015; Anderson et al. 2020; Soley et al. 2024; Costa et al. 2015; Romero et al. 2014

Description: SDMs should be built using input data that are free of substantial errors regarding georeference, also called spatial positional error (i.e., inaccurate location of species occurrences; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024, Araújo et al. 2019).
Violation: Similar to species misidentification, errors in georeferencing may also occur in online biodiversity portals (e.g., GBIF, eBird, iNaturalis), particularly for older records (likely to persist; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). Gábor et al. (2020) also alert for spatial positional errors in recent records due, for example, to data processing issues (e.g., conversion between coordinate reference systems, rounding of coordinate values).
Solutions: Implement partial vetting (Soley et al. 2024)., Remove occurrences without spatial reference., Standardize and clean data for given taxonomic groups and regions (Soley et al. 2024)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.
Justification: Because correlative SDMs rely on extracting predictor values at the exact coordinate pixels of species occurrences, the resulting spatial mismatch leads to a breakdown in the modeled species-environment relationship, as environmental conditions at the recorded locations might differ from those at actual locations (Gábor et al. 2022). The effect of spatial positional error has been largely explored in prediction models, demonstrating that the severity of the resulting prediction errors depends on the modeled spatial resolution, species’ niche breadth, and the degree of local spatial autocorrelation in predictors (Moudrý et al. 2025, Gábor et al. 2020, Tulowiecki et al. 2015, Naimi et al. 2013, Osborne & Leitão 2009). More specifically, fine-scale SDMs, models for specialist species, and for areas with low local spatial association in predictors are among the most severely affected. Gábor et al. (2020) also demonstrated that the presence of spatial positional errors decreases niche overlap compared to a reference model built free of errors, and that increased sample size is not enough to compensate for the detrimental effects of positional error. This suggests that both overestimation and underestimation can occur. For projection models, the consequence of the misidentified niche is likely to be amplified given the added uncertainty of non-analog conditions.

Criterion: Species data covers the environmental extent
Description: As a special case of the criteria “Unbiased species data”, the assumption is that species sampling covers the entire range of the taxon’s environmental tolerances or ecological niche within the study area (for prediction models) or current range (for projection models; Guisan et al. 2025, Araújo et al. 2019). Since SDMs attempt to quantify a species’ environmental niche, the input data used needs to include all possible environments that represent suitable habitats for the modeled species (Guisan et al. 2017).
Violation: This criteria can be violated through violation of the related criteria “Unbiased species data” and “Species data covers the geographic extent”. That is, when the species occurrence is not sampled across all regions of the study area that are suitable for and accessible to the taxon (Araújo et al. 2019). But, as pointed out by Guisan et al. (2025), not all cases of restricted geographic sampling result in violation, since “a subset of the species range could cover the entire range of environmental conditions experienced by a species”. Nevertheless, violation can still occur even when the geographic extent is systematically surveyed if the environmental gradient is not evenly sampled (Pili et al. 2025). Lastly, projection models may be more prone to violation as the conditions used to fit the model may not be representative of future environmental conditions (Pili et al. 2025, Chevalier et al. 2022; also see criteria “Non-novel environmental conditions”).
Solutions: Implement Ensembles of Small Models (ESMs): Instead of one complex model, generate many simple (bivariate) models and average them to avoid overfitting, which is particularly effective for rare or restricted-range species., "Implement Spatially Nested Species Distribution Models (N-SDMs): Combine a broad-scale, coarse-grain model (covering the full range) with a local, fine-grain model (focusing on the study area). (Guisan et al. 2025)", Implement Hierarchical Bayesian Models: These models allow for the integration of data from multiple sources and help separate environmental signals from sampling biases., "Implement Environmental Filtering: Instead of filtering by geography, filter the data to ensure an even distribution across the environmental gradients (e.g. Temperature, Elevation) to ensure all tolerances are represented."
Justification: Environmental conditions that are artificially overrepresented result in overestimation of suitability (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). In turn, conditions that are undersampled or missed can become underestimated due to the niche truncation (i.e., truncated modelled response curves of the species along environmental gradients occur when data does not include all possible conditions that compose the species’ ecological niche; Guisan et al. 2025, Dubos et al. 2022, Chevalier et al. 2021). This impacts both prediction and projection models (Pili et al. 2025, Chevalier et al. 2022).

Description: Much like most statistical methods, SDMs rely on the assumption of independence of observations, that is, that each recorded species presence (or absence) is a unique sample, not influenced by or correlated to nearby records (i.e., not spatially autocorrelated; Guisan & Thuiller 2005).
Violation: This assumption can be easily and frequently violated in ecology. Even if surveys are systematically designed to cover the study extent uniformly and randomly, the species distribution itself is not random (Guisan et al. 2017). Beyond the underlying habitat preferences, a number of ecological and behavioural (intrinsic) factors can result in spatial autocorrelation in species occurrences (or absences), including reproduction, site fidelity, dispersal limitation, home range size, territoriality, and more (Paradinas et al. 2023, Wintle & Bardos 2006). Therefore, surveys may detect the same individual multiple times or multiple individuals of the same population in the same or nearby locations. Alternatively, if intraspecific competition is strong, the detection of one individual at a location may decrease the likelihood of detecting another. Extrinsic factors such as spatially structured environmental processes and patterns, can also lead to spatial autocorrelation in species distribution and therefore lead to violation (Dormann et al. 2007, Wintle & Bardos 2006).
Solutions: Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.
Justification: An SDM aims to explain a species’ pattern of spatial distribution by means of environmental predictors. If the model is successful, no spatial autocorrelation should be left in the model residuals (Guisan et al. 2017). Instead, when the model residuals are spatially autocorrelated, it indicates that intrinsic and/or extrinsic factors were not covered by the model. The main consequence of this violation is an increase in Type I error (false positive) when identifying predictors (Paradinas et al. 2023, Dormann et al. 2007). In terms of prediction error, overestimation of suitable habitat is more likely to occur (e.g., through an inflated estimate of habitat preference; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). But, if important predictors are missing, it can also lead to underestimation of suitable habitat (e.g., through niche truncation; Guisan et al. 2025). This applies to both prediction and projection models, but projection models may suffer further due to the additional temporal and spatio-temporal autocorrelation (Dormann et al. 2007).
Citations: Guisan & Thuiller 2005; Guisan et al. 2017; Paradinas et al. 2023; Wintle & Bardos 2006; Dormann et al. 2007; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Guisan et al. 2025

Therefore, surveys may detect the same individual multiple times or multiple individuals of the same population in the same or nearby locations. Alternatively, if intraspecific competition is strong, the detection of one individual at a location may decrease the likelihood of detecting another. Extrinsic factors such as spatially structured environmental processes and patterns, can also lead to spatial autocorrelation in species distribution and therefore lead to violation (Dormann et al. 2007, Wintle & Bardos 2006).
Solutions: Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.
Justification: An SDM aims to explain a species’ pattern of spatial distribution by means of environmental predictors. If the model is successful, no spatial autocorrelation should be left in the model residuals (Guisan et al. 2017). Instead, when the model residuals are spatially autocorrelated, it indicates that intrinsic and/or extrinsic factors were not covered by the model. The main consequence of this violation is an increase in Type I error (false positive) when identifying predictors (Paradinas et al. 2023, Dormann et al. 2007). In terms of prediction error, overestimation of suitable habitat is more likely to occur (e.g., through an inflated estimate of habitat preference; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). But, if important predictors are missing, it can also lead to underestimation of suitable habitat (e.g., through niche truncation; Guisan et al. 2025). This applies to both prediction and projection models, but projection models may suffer further due to the additional temporal and spatio-temporal autocorrelation (Dormann et al. 2007).

Description: This criteria describes the assumption that if a species is present at a sampled site, it will be detected.
Violation: Unless sampling effort is sufficiently large, species often remain undetected at occupied sites (Lahoz-Monfort et al. 2013). Imperfect detection can happen for a variety of reasons, including survey conditions and species behaviour (e.g., survey window does not align with the species seasonal or daily activity peaks, limited visual and acoustic detection ranges, meteorological conditions; Tyre et al. 2003).
Solutions: Consider using occupancy models (e.g. Erickson & Smith 2021; Comte & Grenoulliet 2013)., Consider data integration and fusion., Consider using advance modelling frameworks such as Joint Species Dsitribution Models (JSDMs).
Justification: Imperfect detection results in classifying true presences as false absences. Similar to the presence of spatial positional error and biased sampling, this creates a misalignment between the species' actual distribution and the training data. In this case, the presence of numerous false absence points in otherwise suitable environments leads to underestimation (Lahoz-Monfort et al. 2013). If detection probability is structured (e.g., species is more easily detected in open fields than closed forests), the model will overestimate suitability in the areas where detectability is high and underestimate it in areas with low detectability (e.g., Gu & Swihart 2004). This affects both prediction and projection models.
Citations: Lahoz-Monfort et al. 2013; Tyre et al. 2003; Erickson & Smith 2021; Comte & Grenoulliet 2013; Gu & Swihart 2004

Description: The spatial resolution of predictors should match the resolution at which the response variable is affected by the predictors (Araújo et al. 2019, Wiens et al. 2010).
Violation: This criteria is violated by mismatches in spatial scales between the species responses and the predictor variables. Spatial mismatches typically happen in two directions: when predictors are too coarse to capture a fine-scale process (e.g., use of a coarse global climate variable to explain a species that is limited by microclimate availability; Chauvier et al. 2022), or when predictors are too fine to capture a broad landscape process (e.g., use of fine-scale vegetation cover data to explain a species that is limited by availability of contiguous forest cover). Lastly, Bradter et al. (2012) point out that a predictor may influence a species at more than one scale, so violation can also occur by ignoring potentially meaningful scales, or by the lack of available data at the relevant resolution (Guisan et al. 2017).
Solutions: Identify appropriate scales of predictors (e.g. Bradter et al. 2012)., Test relevant covariates at multiple scales.
Justification: When models are built using predictors that are too spatially coarse, overestimation of suitable areas is commonly reported due to the model smoothing over fine scale conditions that are suboptimal for the species (e.g., Anselmetto et al. 2025, Wiens et al. 2010). Although less discussed in the literature, models built using predictors that are too spatially coarse may also underestimate specialized requirements via the same over-smoothing mechanism, but instead, resulting in missed unique environmental tolerances (Guisan et al. 2017; also see criteria “Species data covers the environmental extent”). Alternatively, models built using predictors that are too spatially fine may result in highly fragmented and noisy distribution maps and thus underestimate suitability. This effect can be more pronounced in the case of projection models, amplified by differences between the training and extrapolated area and/or time (Manzoor et al. 2018). The magnitude of the prediction error, however, also depends on the magnitude of the deviations, with significant impacts expected beyond a 10-fold coarsening (Seo et al. 2008, Guisan et al. 2007). Additionally, resolution can interact with other processes, such as species niche breadth and landscape heterogeneity (e.g., Chauvier et al. 2022, Connor et al. 2017).

Description: The temporal resolution of predictors should match the resolution at which the response variable is affected by the predictors (Araújo et al. 2019, Wiens et al. 2010).

Justification: Models that fail to account for important short-term events may overestimate suitability (Stewart et al. 2021), and models that incorrectly rely solely on long-term or average conditions may underestimate suitability (e.g., in the case of migratory species; Araújo et al. 2019, Batalden et al. 2007).

Criterion: Uncertainty in predictor variables is accounted for
Description: Uncertainty in predictor variables is an inherent factor of SDMs (McInerny & Purves 2011). Since it is essentially impossible to guarantee zero errors in mapped environmental predictors – which can be introduced in a variety of ways, including instrument measurement error, spatial scaling, geo-registration, interpolation (Araújo et al. 2019, McInerny & Purves 2011, Barry & Elith 2006) – SDMs should include quantification of sources of uncertainty. Ideally, modellers should quantify the effects of the relevant predictor uncertainties on SDM outputs; at a minimum, likely sources of uncertainty should be acknowledged and their possible effects on SDM results discussed (Araújo et al. 2019). Additionally, when using model products with inherent uncertainties (e.g., climate change models), those should also be accounted for (Cheaib et al. 2012).
Violation: This criteria is violated when modellers use predictor variables with no consideration of errors and uncertainty (Araújo et al. 2019).
Solutions: Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.
Justification: When uncertainties in predictor variables are unaccounted for, they can lead to bias in the estimates of the model's parameters. Specifically, when violation leads to a predictor variable that fails to capture fine-scale variation (i.e., attenuation bias) and the species is known to respond to particular conditions (e.g., a strict physiological temperature constraint), both underestimation and overestimation of suitable habitat is reported to occur in prediction and projection models owing to a flattened response curve (Stoklosa et al. 2015, McInerny & Purves 2011). In the same way that an overly smooth predictor layer can miss identifying specialized habitat requirements, thus leading to underestimation, it can also incorrectly associate species presences to other more widespread conditions, leading to overestimation. Violation can also lead to a loss of power (i.e., ability to determine which predictor variables are most important; Stoklosa et al. 2015) when there are strong spatial patterns in predictor variable errors. As the relationships between variables may change across space and/or time, this can also lead to prediction errors (Barry and Elith 2006). While ignoring predictor uncertainty introduces attenuation bias, the severity of its effect are likely to be weakened in the following cases: for prediction models where the uncertainty is systematic and uniform across the study area (Barry and Elith 2006); for generalist species with wide tolerances (Velásquez-Tibatá et al. 2016); when modeling biodiversity trends at ecoregional or continental scales (Seo et al. 2008).
Citations: McInerny & Purves 2011; Araújo et al. 2019; Barry & Elith 2006; Cheaib et al. 2012; Stoklosa et al. 2015; Velásquez-Tibatá et al. 2016; Seo et al. 2008

Criterion: Model complexity and structure are appropriate (under fit models)
Description: Building an SDMs involves fitting a correlative relationship between the biological occurrence data and predictor variables, described by a model approach, structure and parameters. Complex models may perform better when the goal is to explain the data; but when predicting or projecting, overly complex models can lead to overfitting and poor robustness and accuracy (Brun et al. 2019, Merow et al. 2014, Braunisch et al. 2013; but also see Evans et al. 2013). Therefore, the choice of model complexity should be carefully assessed and alternatives compared (Araújo et al. 2019,, Merow et al. 2014).
Violation: This criteria can be violated both by building ‘under fit’ models – where simplifications are made in the formulation, structure and complexity of the model – or ‘over fit’ models – excessively flexible and overly complex. This can also happen through violation of the criteria “Statistical methods and algorithms employed are appropriate” and/or “Predictor variables are appropriately reduced, if applicable”. For the special case of ‘under fit’ models due to missing key predictors, see criteria “Species data covers the environmental extent”.
Solutions: Comparing a range of models (predictive performance) & response shapes (Ramampiandra et al. 2023)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.
Justification: ‘Under fit’ models are commonly related to overestimation of suitable habitat as they fail to appropriately capture species-environmental relationships (e.g., a linear model fails to represent commonly unimodal relationships to temperature). In turn, the special case of ‘under fit’ models due to missing key predictors can lead to underestimation due to the niche truncation (Guisan et al. 2025, Dubos et al. 2022, Chevalier et al. 2021). These prediction errors apply to both prediction and projection models.

Criterion: Model complexity and structure are appropriate (over fit models)
Description: The Eltonian noise hypothesis states that local biotic interactions do not alter species’ environmental niches at larger scales, only introduce statistical noise. Instead, species niche is assumed to be dominantly determined by climate (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). Most SDMs rely on this hypothesis and thus, often only include abiotic variables as predictors. Yet, biotic interactions are among the reasons why a species may not be at equilibrium with their environment (Richmond et al. 2010, Jeschke & Strayer 2008).
Violation: There is growing evidence that this assumption can be frequently violated, supported by improved SDMs when biotic interactions are included (e.g., Fern et al. 2019, Boulangeat et al. 2012, Godsoe & Harmon 2012, Suttle et al. 2007). In some cases (e.g., boreal caribou, wolf, and moose; Boutin et al. 2012), there is evidence that competition and/or predation restrict the distribution of species (Poggiato et al. 2025). In other cases, it is clear that mutualism and/or symbiosis allow species to persist. By ignoring biotic interactions, SDMs may capture the Grinnellian (fundamental bioclimatic) niche instead of the Eltonian (realized biotic) niche (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). However, Godsoe & Harmon (2012) highlight that violation of this assumption is not universal. Instead, it depends on the species, type of biotic interaction, and modelling method (Araújo & Luoto 2007). Additionally, the chances of violating this criteria increase with the extent of the study region (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024).
Solutions: Comparing a range of models (predictive performance) & response shapes (Ramampiandra et al. 2023)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.
Justification: ‘Over fit’ prediction models often lead to underestimation of suitable habitat by ascribing pattern to noise and resulting in highly specific species-environmental relationships (Merow et al. 2014).

Description: SDMs assume there is no collinearity between predictors (i.e., non-independence of predictors via a linear relationship; Dormann et al. 2013).

Criterion: Modelling and parameter uncertainty are dealt with
Description: SDMs have multiple sources of model and parameter value uncertainty that should be assessed and incorporated into the analysis (Araújo et al. 2019). Beyond data uncertainty (see criteria “Unbiased species data” and “Uncertainty in predictor variables is accounted for”), one of the largest sources of variation in SDM predictions can be attributed to the algorithm of choice, particularly when projecting to future climate scenarios (Watling et al. 2015, Buisson et al. 2010). Several decisions around model parameterization – mainly those related to model complexity and flexibility – also affect predictions and can thus contribute to uncertainty (Araújo & Guisan 2006). Additional sources of model and parameter uncertainty may include alternative model structures, initial conditions, and parameter estimation or values (Beale & Lennon 2012). For the related case of structural model misspecification, such as omitting key biological or environmental processes from the model equations, see criteria “All predictors relevant for the species response are included”.
Violation: This criteria is violated if the most important sources of uncertainty in model and parameter value are not addressed or comprehensively characterized (see Araújo et al. 2019 for a summary of approaches for addressing uncertainty).
Solutions: Spend effort on reducing SDM extrapolation rather than improving model fit (e.g. fitting species data over a broader range of environmental conditions). Description: The performance of a model can be assessed in many different ways. Araújo et al. (2019) suggests three dimensions of evaluation: realism, accuracy, and generality. Which dimension(s) to evaluate will depend on the question and model objective but typically, evaluation metrics (i.e., statistical tools used to evaluate model outputs) are concerned with model accuracy and generality. In turn, defining which model performance metrics are appropriate and exhaustively summarize model performance depends primarily on the structure of the species occurrence data (i.e., presence-absence or presence-only) and on the type of the response variable (e.g., count, presence-absence; Guisan et al. 2017). Other factors such as the robustness of the metric to species prevalence (i.e., the proportion of sampled sites where the species is present versus absent) or the requirement for a threshold-dependent versus -independent metric given the research objective should also be taken into account. For guidance on selecting appropriate metrics, see Guisan et al. (2017).
Violation: This criteria can be violated in multiple ways. For example, a projection model violates this criteria if it fails to evaluate its generality (Araújo et al. 2019). A model built using presence-only and pseudo-absence data violates this criteria if computing statistics such as AUC (area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve) and TSS (true skill statistic) that require the use of true absences to calculate the confusion matrix (Guillaumot et al. 2019). Jiménez-Valverde (2011) also suggests that “[w]hen the potential distribution is the goal of the research, the AUC is not an appropriate performance measure because the weight of commission errors is much lower than that of omission errors”.
Solutions: Selecting the Right Metrics: Different metrics (AUC, TSS, Kappa, Tjur's R2), etc.) evaluate different aspects of model performance (e.g. discrimination, calibration, accuracy) and respond differently to factors like species prevalence., "Consider Ecological Plausibility: Do not just focus on a high performance score; ensure that the model's relationships with environmental variables are ecologically relevant and make sense based on existing knowledge of the species (e.g. expected temperature responses).", Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.
Justification: When model assessment fails to employ the appropriate evaluation metrics, it risks not capturing or inappropriately assessing prediction errors and other potential shortcomings in the model performance. In other words, the incorrect metric will not cause a prediction error, but it can compromise the ability to correctly detect prediction error. For example, when modelling rare species, inappropriate metrics may inflate the sense of accuracy and miss the detection of underestimation or overestimation (Allouche et al. 2006). Alternatively, in the case of modelling potential distribution, an evaluation metric that weights false negatives and false positives equally will be misleading, as overestimation is unlikely a concern (Jiménez-Valverde 2011). In the case of applying a presence-absence metric to a presence-only data, evaluation results might suggest the model is overestimating suitable habitat (i.e., by inflating commission error; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024, Lobo et al. 2008).
Citations: Araújo et al. 2019; Guisan et al. 2017; Guillaumot et al. 2019; Jiménez-Valverde 2011; Allouche et al. 2006; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Lobo et al. 2008

Criterion: Setting an appropriate threshold, if applicable
Description: Some SDM approaches require transforming continuous habitat suitability predictions into a binary (presence/absence) map, whether it is a requirement for an evaluation metric derived from the confusion matrix (e.g., True Skill Statistic) or for interpretation purposes (e.g., to support conservation decisions). This transformation requires defining a threshold, above and below which a species/habitat is to be considered present/suitable and absent/unsuitable, respectively. The choice of threshold is known to directly influence the balance between omission and commission errors (Guisan et al. 2013, Benito et al. 2013, Liu et al. 2005). Therefore, it is assumed that the appropriate threshold is set by modellers based on the acceptable ecological stakes of omission versus commission errors (given the applied objective), and on the structure of the species data (Abdel-Moniem et al. 2025, Liu et al. 2005).
Violation: The main way this criteria is violated is by relying on default threshold values, such as the subjective but widely used 0.5 threshold (Liu et al. 2005). Selecting a threshold value without consideration of the quality and prevalence of the species occurrence data can also lead to violation (Liu et al. 2005).
Solutions: Compare multiple thresholding methods (see Abdel-Moniem et al. 2025; Guisan et al. (2025).
Justification: Raising or lowering the threshold leads to a trade-off between commission and omission errors (e.g., Benito et al. 2013). A threshold value that is too low relative to the ideal results in the classification of low suitability sites as "suitable". The consequence is overestimation. In contrast, a threshold value that is too high relative to the ideal results in the exclusion of otherwise suitable sites. The consequence is underestimation. This affects both prediction and projection models.
Citations: Guisan et al. 2013; Benito et al. 2013; Liu et al. 2005; Abdel-Moniem et al. 2025; Guisan et al. 2025

Description: The assumption of a projection model is that it is able to accurately predict species responses under novel conditions. The paradox is that, in most cases, validation of projection models is not possible as future data does not yet exist or data might be severely limited (e.g., during early stages of a biological invasion; Araújo et al. 2005). Therefore, modelers must instead demonstrate that extrapolation risk has been minimized (e.g., Mesgaran et al. 2014; also see related criteria “Extrapolation approach is appropriate”) and that response curves conform to biological and physiological evidence. Modelers may also test predictions via temporal hindcasting (e.g., Martínez-Meyer et al. 2004), by simulating virtual species (e.g., Meynard et al. 2019), and/or using spatial transferability approaches (e.g., Charney et al. 2021, Roberts et al. 2017).
Violation: Directly validating projection models to determine whether or not violation has occurred is not feasible (Araújo et al. 2005). But, given future times and/or different locations are likely to experience novel conditions than the ones considered in the model training, violation of this criteria can easily occur (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). The risk of violation is higher if the criteria “Extrapolation approach is appropriate” is violated, and/or if modelers fail to evaluate response curves or implement indirect validation approaches. Additionally, violation of the criteria “Model complexity and structure are appropriate” may also increase the risk of violation (Charney et al. 2021, Yates et al. 2018).
Solutions: Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.
Justification: While violation of this criteria is certain to lead to prediction error, the direction of prediction error depends on the ecological and modelling context. Also see criteria “Extrapolation approach is appropriate” and “Model complexity and structure are appropriate” for more.

Criterion: Model outputs scaling into absolute probability of presence is appropriate, if applicable
Description: When an SDM is built without true absence information, its output can only represent relative suitability (i.e., suitability relative to the local background environment; Guillera-Arroita et al. 2014, Phillips & Elith 2013). If the modeller or end-users intend to compare the outputs of an SDM across different species and/or locations, outputs need to be expressed in absolute probability of presence. Therefore, meaningful comparisons require the transformation of outputs into absolute probability of presence through a scaling function (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024, Phillips & Elith 2013). This transformation relies on using prevalence and/or local abundance data to parameterize the scaling parameters.
Violation: This criteria can be easily violated as prevalence and/or abundance data rarely exists across large extents and multiple species, preventing estimation of scaling parameters (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). Thus, modellers that rely on default values of scaling parameters or on presence-background data to estimate scaling parameters violate this criteria (Guillera-Arroita et al. 2014). Additionally, violation can also occur simply by failing to scale the SDM output altogether.
Solutions: Estimates of occupancy or abundance can be used to set the scaling parameters rather than relying on default values (Soley et al . 2024)., Make assumptions regarding scaling parameters for sets of species with similar natural histories (Soley et al . 2024)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.
Justification: If this criteria is violated, comparison between SDM outputs across different species and/or locations will be nonsensical (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). Since relative suitability represents suitability relative to the local background environment, a relative suitability value of 0.8 in a highly degraded landscape does not compare to the same suitability value in a landscape where good quality habitat is highly available. While violation will not lead to prediction errors, it will impact the conclusion of comparisons (e.g., lead to severe misallocations of conservation resources).
Citations: Guillera-Arroita et al. 2014; Phillips & Elith 2013; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024
